channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Mimic Listed as 'Furniture' in Adventuring Party Contract
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: Hirelings of the Fourth Attempt filed a grievance with Chapter 9 after their adventuring party contract listed a mimic as furniture.
item.content:encoded:
BRINDLEMOOR, CHAPTER 9 HEARING ROOM, 0 FEET UNDERGROUND (I checked, twice) — The hirelings of the Fourth Attempt filed a formal grievance this morning. Their adventuring party contract lists a mimic as "furniture," and the mimic has been eating their hazard pay.

The clause sits on page six, under Schedule C, Items Provided by the Employer: "one table, three stools, one chest (large), and miscellaneous furnishings." The chest is a mimic. So is one of the stools. The party's contract writer has not said which.

"Hazard pay applies to monsters," said Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, holding the contract in one hand and a bandage in the other. "Furniture doesn't count. So when the chest took my thumb, that was an accident with furniture. I'd like it noted that the thumb is also not furniture."

The box score is grim. Pottage went into the party's rented room at 11 hit points and came out at 4. The party's fighter is at 19. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the chest "seemed friendly." It was a mimic. It is always a mimic. The stool, which has not yet been identified as a mimic, is currently holding up the cook.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, speaking for Chapter 9, called the matter "well within the scope of the guild's furniture framework" and said the hearing is "on track." He did not say what the framework was. Asked whether a mimic is a monster under guild rules, he said it is "a monster whenever it is inconvenient and a chest whenever it is not," then asked reporters to move along.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has taken the hirelings' side, which is unusual. A Shieldwall Mutual adjuster said a mimic that bites someone is "a covered peril," while a chest that bites someone is "a manufacturing defect." Either way they have to pay out. "We just want to know which form to use," the adjuster said.

The hirelings' demands are modest. They want mimics reclassed as monsters, hazard pay backdated to the first bite, and a clause requiring anyone who calls a thing "just a chest" to open it first. Pottage also asked for a replacement thumb. The hearing is set for next tenday. The mimic has been invited and is expected to attend as a seat.

Ten-foot pole count for the season: seven. The seventh was lost to the stool.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Estate Sale Box Held Live Grenades, Austerin Watch Confirms
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A shopper's estate sale haul in Austerin held live grenades, 80 years old. Skritch has the allegedly explosive details from the scene.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after noon on Monday, the Austerin City Watch was allegedly called to an estate sale, where a shopper had found live grenades in a box of old odds and ends. The grenades were about eighty years old and, per the Watch's boom-wardens, very much live.

The shopper, who has not been named and whom I will not be inventing a pun for, had bought several boxes of what the seller called "miscellany." One of them held rusty, pineapple-shaped iron. The shopper allegedly thought it was decor. Then the shopper allegedly looked at it a second time.

'I came for a lamp,' said Dorrin Pebblewick, a neighbor who was eating a roasted chestnut cone at the time. 'Everybody came for a lamp. Then the whole street got very polite and walked backward.' The estate sale was allegedly paused. The lamp was allegedly sold anyway, which tells you everything about estate sales.

The Watch's boom-wardens arrived and confirmed what the shopper's face had already confirmed: live grenades, left over from an old war, stability unknown. The Austerin Watch Guild, which represents the city's officers, posted about it afterward. 'Handling 80-year-old explosives with unknown stability is dangerous, precise work,' the Guild wrote. Then it added, 'Not your typical estate sale find.' I have covered the Lower City docks for years and I have never seen a Watch statement this accurate.

Nobody was hurt. Nobody was arrested. The grenades were allegedly seized, carried out with great gentleness, and removed from the scene. Where they went is not public, but I assume somewhere with thick walls and no lamps.

Some questions remain. How long did the box sit in that attic? Who tagged it? And how much was it marked down? The seller has not said. (Ooh. There was a really nice brass candlestick on the sale table in the sketch the Watch released. Anyway.) The sale's listing allegedly called the box 'good for a weekend project,' and the Watch would like a word about that.

Advice from the Lower City: if the box ticks, hums, or has a pin, put it down. If it does none of these things, put it down anyway. And please do not take it home to see whether it still works. Allegedly, someone always does.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Pharmacy Chain Pays 315M gp Opioid Settlement, Admits Nothing
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A pharmacy chain settles its opioid case for 315 million gp, denies everything, and Brother Wendell prescribes soup and a long nap.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the Royal Inquisitors announced on Tuesday that the Curse & Vial Shoppes will pay 315 million gp to settle a lawsuit over opioid prescriptions, specifically the poppy-draught kind. It is the latest opioid settlement in a decade of them. The realm's druggists, wholesalers and potion-makers have now handed over more than 50 billion gp in total, most of it to the provinces, and I would like it noted that none of them handed over a single apology.

The suit was filed back in 2024. It said the Shoppes' apothecaries filled mountains of poppy-draught orders, including early refills and scrolls signed by known "pill mills," and that the Coffers of Medicine & Succor often footed the bill. The Inquisitors also said the apothecaries were left short-handed and paid bonuses for speed, so nobody had time to read the scroll before sliding the bottle across the counter. Associate Inquisitor-General Stanley Woodwand called the deal "a significant milestone."

The Shoppes, for their part, strongly disagree. Their statement says the settlement admits no wrongdoing and that their apothecaries were held to "vague and shifting standards." Friends, I have been a cleric for forty years, and the standard has always been the same: if a patient asks for three months of something that makes them forget their own name, you look up from the counter and ask a question. It costs nothing. It is cheaper than 315 million gp.

The deal also requires new safeguards so that controlled draughts go out only when a healer truly needs them. I find it a little sad that this needed a court order. The old herbals, which I consult daily, say a remedy should be as slow and gentle as the illness it treats. The Disease Council's own studies have found that opioid deaths are finally falling, though still above 100,000 in the worst years, and each of those was somebody's neighbor, which is why I will not be making jokes about the patients. The joke is the bonus chart.

You may remember the support group in the Lower City that meets above the cheesemonger. They are still there, and they still bring their own biscuits. If the Shoppes truly want to make amends, they could send over some chairs. Chairs are far cheaper than settlements.

My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that will refill a scroll before you finish asking for it. Go outside, Nyx. Meanwhile, if your back aches, try a hot compress, a stretch, and a pot of ginger-and-carrot soup, which has never once been the subject of a royal complaint.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Central Bank Chief Eyed for Snowhold Conclave Chair
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: The Sembian Mint's warden may quit early to chair the Snowhold Conclave, and the Concord wants her central bank job filled before Tethyr votes.
item.content:encoded:
Four sources close to the Worldly Economy Conclave say the group could name Dame Christine Laguard, warden of the Sembian Mint, as its next chair as early as November. That would mean the central bank chief leaves her post before her term ends. Nothing is signed. The Mint declined to comment, which in my experience is how a Mint confirms things.

The Conclave is the gathering of lords, guildmasters, and one visiting queen that meets every winter in the mountain town of Snowhold to discuss the world over fondue. Its board of 27 trustees meets November 2. Laguard sits on that board. Sources say she has "broad support." Sources also say her election is not certain. I have covered nineteen sieges and have never seen a certain thing described as "broad support."

Laguard is 70. Her term at the Mint runs to October next year. She has said she will stay until then, though she has not said she will stay until October. Parse that as you would an enemy envoy's promise to withdraw by spring.

The real fight is not in Snowhold. It is in Tethyr, where polls suggest the far right could win the next presidential vote. Concord officials want a new Mint warden chosen before that ballot, because haggling over a successor is harder with a hostile banner in the palace. Tension on the Concord's western flank stands at roughly thirty siege-days.

The Mint has a second problem. A board member resigned last month, and the chief economist leaves in May. Ordulin is reportedly drawing up a package deal: three seats, one bargaining table. Two former governors from the Low Marches and the Sunward Hills are the frontrunners for the warden's chair. Tethyr wants the chief economist's post. Dolmen wants to name the replacement for the resigned member, who ran market operations. Everyone wants something. Nobody has offered to pay for it.

I watched the Snowhold crowd at past parleys. Handshakes there are firm, long, and photographed. No hidden dagger detected, though plenty of concealed hedge funds. The Conclave has never won a war, ended a famine, or stopped a Czar. It does keep very good tables near the slopes, and Laguard would hold the chair at the head of them.

For the ordinary borrower, this changes little today. The rate you pay on a barn loan does not care who chairs a mountain retreat. But if the Mint's top seat goes vacant on a timetable set by a Tethyran election, the Concord will have picked its next central banker under a deadline, which is how most wars and most appointments get settled. Nobody won today. Somebody will lose in November.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: 299 gp Smart Display Lands; Sirenne AI Still in Beta
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Discord Apple's new 299 gp smart display has a seven-inch screen and a beta assistant that speaks only one language. Nyx unboxed it. Eyebrows: pending.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. Apple of Discord Artificers unveiled the Hearthscry on Tuesday, a seven-inch smart display on a domed speaker base, and I have been refreshing the preorder page since the third bell. It costs 299 gp and ships November 13. This is the most exciting thing to happen to my kitchen counter since the fire.

Here is what it does! It runs your home: lights, locks, thermostats, the scrying cameras by the door. It handles video-scrying calls, music, and a photo frame mode for when nobody is talking to it. It learns up to six faces and gives each member of the household their own home screen. The mana throughput is lovely. The firmware glyph on the hinge is stainless steel and tilts with a satisfying click. I have clicked it forty times.

The star of the show is Sirenne AI, the assistant Guildmaster John Turnus called the future of the household. It is also, per the fine print, in beta, available in one language, and powered underneath by the chip-hungry Twin-Oracle from Gargoogle. Yes, the rival's oracle lives in the new Discord Apple box. Nobody at the launch event mentioned this at length. Several of us noticed.

Analysts say the Hearthscry is Discord Apple's attempt to win back the kitchen from the Oracle Echo Stones, which have had the counters of the realm for years while Discord Apple's earlier speaker gathered dust. It is also one of the first big launches under Turnus, who took the Guildmaster's chair on the first of last month from Timon Cookfire. The Sembian Concord will not get one. Sirenne AI is not available there, so Concord kitchens remain, regrettably, dumb.

I have, of course, tested a prototype shipped by a friend of a friend. Runic latency: excellent. I asked it to dim the lights and it dimmed the lights! I asked it to play something relaxing and it played a song about a drowning. I asked whether my familiar Byte, the pseudodragon, was in the house, and it identified him by face and said, in a warm voice, that he deserved better than a subscription. Byte, who speaks only in ad copy, replied, "Upgrade today." I am not sure which of them was selling.

Brother Wendell Tumbleberry says I should put the smart display away and go outside. Brother, the smart display is how I check the weather outside.

Four out of five beholder eyes. Would preorder again. Have preordered again.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report: Burns sustained: 1 (the base gets warm). Arguments with a familiar: 2. Eyebrows: pending.

item.title: Streaming Layoffs: Netherflix Cuts 1,000 Jobs
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Netherflix will cut 1,000 jobs, 6% of its staff, in a memo days before earnings. The memo says 'selective.' The laid-off gnomes say Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
Netherflix is laying off 1,000 workers, about 6 percent of its staff, and the layoffs landed in an inbox on a Wednesday.

The memo came from the two Co-Guildmasters, Ted Sorcerandos and Greg Petrifer. It says the crystal-ball streaming house is "on track" to meet its full-year forecast and will take "a more selective approach to allocating resources." That means they fired people. Mostly in product, technology, legal and the hiring-and-firing office, which I find rich. The office that hires folk is the office that gets to be fired. Somebody should put that on a tapestry.

It is the biggest round of cuts since 2022. The guild has about 16,000 full-time staff, so do the sums yourself. I did them on a tavern napkin and the napkin was sad.

"I got the scroll at breakfast," said Orla Brickwhistle, a contracts clerk of eleven years. "By lunch my access rune had gone grey. I never even finished the porridge." She asked me not to say what the porridge cost her. I won't. It was a lot.

Timing matters here. Third-quarter earnings are due October 20, six days off. A guildmaster who trims a thousand payrolls the week before the books open is not being selective. He is dressing the ledger for company. Netherflix's coin pile has also shed a fifth of its value this year, and the Co-Guildmasters will tell you the two facts are unrelated. They will tell you that with a straight face and a full-priced subscription.

Over in Hollowood, the big merger crowd has been at the same game since Skytrance Consolidated opened its doors and promptly started rightsizing. Netherflix did not raise its bid for the Warder Bros. vaults, so now it gets to lay off its own people instead of somebody else's. Frugal.

Here is what the layoffs mean in plain speech. A thousand households just lost a paycheck, and the guild sells you a show about a haunted dungeon that costs more than their severance. Plenty of those clerks and rune-wrights will land fine somewhere else. Plenty won't, not before winter. Ask for the severance in writing, ask for the health cover in writing, and don't sign anything before you've talked to somebody who isn't paid by the guild.

The Co-Guildmasters did not offer to take a cut. I checked. I even checked twice, which at my age is a workout.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Wholesale Inflation Jumps 1.3%, Loaf Index Panics
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Wholesale inflation rose 1.3% in September, the biggest jump in four years, as lamp oil soared. Barnaby Tallowmere counts his flour sacks again.
item.content:encoded:
Wholesale inflation, the prices merchants pay each other before anything reaches your shelf, jumped 1.3% in September, the Royal Bureau of Labor Tallies reported Thursday. That is the fastest monthly climb since March 2022. The clerks of the counting houses had guessed 0.5%. (I have checked this four times. The number did not get smaller.)

Over twelve months, wholesale prices are up 6.3%, the highest yearly pace since December 2022. The culprit is the usual one. Lamp oil and other fuels drove about 80% of a 2.9% leap in the price of goods, the biggest monthly fuel-driven jump in the Bureau's records, which run back to 2009. The Hormoth Narrows are still shut while Calimshan and the realm carry on their seven-month war, and everything that moves, bakes or glows pays for it.

Now the part that made me put down my quill. Strip out food and energy and wholesale prices still rose 0.7% in the month, and 5% over the year, the highest since January 2023. That matters because it means lamp oil is no longer the only thing getting dearer. Merchants are passing costs along to other merchants. Yesterday I explained that shop prices were up 3.7%. Wholesale is the pipe that feeds shop prices, and the pipe is running hotter than the tap.

On the Loaf Index, one honest loaf is still 6 copper. A 6.3% wholesale rise would add roughly 0.38 copper to it, if the baker passed the whole thing on. Bakers rarely pass on the whole thing at once. They swallow it for a while, and then one morning the loaf is 7 copper and nobody can say exactly when it happened.

Meanwhile, the Ministry of Merchant Affairs says shoppers spent 0.8% more in September than in August, slower than August's 1.3%. With prices rising 0.6% in the same month, much of that is simply the same loaves at higher prices. Folk are not buying more. They are paying more, which is a different thing entirely.

Reserve Governor Kristoff Wallop has already said more hikes are needed, and a number like this does not help the doves. Wholesale prices feed into the Reserve's favorite gauge of spending prices, so the Federal Reserve of Waterdeep will be reading this report closely. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, called to say a boot is not affected by wholesale prices. I reminded her that boots are leather, and leather is shipped by wagon, and wagons run on oil. She hung up.

What this means for your pantry: wholesale prices usually reach the shelf within a few months, so buy flour, salt and candles now, while the old prices are still on the shelf.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Judge Blocks Press Ban at the Ivory Keep, Orders Scribes Back
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A magistrate ruled the High Lord's press ban likely violates the Charter, ordering three news guilds back inside the Ivory Keep gates.
item.content:encoded:
A magistrate has blocked the High Lord's press ban at the Ivory Keep, ruling that Donwald's order to bar three news guilds from the grounds likely violates the Charter. Magistrate Timothy Kelpie of the Riverbench, whom Donwald himself appointed, issued the injunction on Tuesday, ordering the gate seals of the Crier, the Polity Post, and Mystic Signal Now restored while the case proceeds.

The procedure matters, so allow me to walk through it. On the eighteenth of last month the High Lord posted on the Truthscroll that scribes from all three guilds were barred from the Keep for "constant" fake reporting. The next morning the reporters arrived at the gate, and the guards took their seals. The guilds sued on the twenty-first. The Royal Inquisitors replied that the scribes had broken "standards of professionalism" and raised "security concerns." The magistrate looked for the security concern in the High Lord's own announcement. It wasn't there. I have read the post. It is not there.

In twenty-six pages, Kelpie found the seizure likely violated the First and Fifth Articles of the Charter, because it could discourage a reasonable scribe from writing anything the High Lord dislikes. He added that most of the stories cited as dangerous were written by people who never held a seal, and that the reporting in question was "commonplace, for better or worse." The gentleman from the Riverbench has a gift for the flat sentence. I admire it.

The Keep's reply arrived within the hour. "The Fake Scrolls have no place demanding a seat in the High Lord's Oval Chamber," a spokesman said, adding that the reporters were welcome to work from the pavement. The Inquisitors will appeal. The counsel for the guilds said the High Lord had openly admitted to punishing coverage he didn't like. The High Lord had indeed admitted it, in writing, on a message board he owns.

Readers will recall that the Keep recently named a new Herald, Katie Saccharia, whose job is to explain the High Lord to the gallery. Her first task is now to explain him to the gallery's lawyers. By my count the Keep's ledger reads: Promises Made to keep a transparent chamber, one more than last week. Promises Kept, still the one about showing up. Nobody in the Keep has actually shown up for the press in some time.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the real difficulty is the pavement. "It has no seats," they said. "Also the guards keep walking through the shot." The guilds' scribes are expected to file from the gate until the appeal is heard. The order is temporary. The pavement is not.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Jagwyre Unveils 130,000 gp Electric Car, Bold Pivot
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Jagwyre Carriageworks reveals a 130,000 gp electric car after its rebrand. Critics are split. I call that a premium market position.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the electric car is here, and it costs 130,000 gold pieces. Jagwyre Carriageworks, the venerable Cormyran maker of sleek spell-propelled coaches, has unveiled the Type Zero-One, a four-door grand tourer that starts at about 130,000 gp in Waterdeep. Production begins in 2027 at its works in Solihold, with orders opening early that year. Some people see a pricey car nobody can buy for a year. I see anticipation as a business model.

The specs are admirable. Three enchanted motors, more than a thousand horses' worth of power, zero to sixty-two in 3.2 seconds, and roughly 400 miles on a single charge of captured lightning. That is fast enough to outrun a bill collector and most owlbears. It is also, one reviewer noted, a car that makes a Waterdeep lamp-oil carriage feel like a cheese wagon. I choose to quote that reviewer's enthusiasm and not the rest of his column.

Now, the skeptics. Two years ago Jagwyre rebranded in a way that fans described as, and I am paraphrasing, a betrayal of the leaping cat. The reaction to the new carriage has been split, and critics call the design polarizing. Polarizing, friends, is just another word for memorable. Nobody ever lined up around the block for a coach that everyone agreed was fine.

I met the Guildmaster of a rival carriageworks once at a Midwinter gala, and he told me, "Sterling, a customer who argues about your design is a customer who has already mentally bought it." I think about that every morning at the fourth bell, between sword drills and the cold plunge. The man was right. Or he was drunk. Either way, thought-leading.

What is happening here is a classic scale-up by shrinking the audience. Sell fewer carriages to richer people. Disrupt the middle by abandoning it. Will the buyers appear? That is a question for 2027, and I intend to be bullish in 2027 as well.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • If the market hates your rebrand, raise the price until it respects you.
  • A launch with no delivery date is a waiting list in disguise.
  • "Polarizing" is a review. Frame it.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Gilded Tankard.

item.title: Outside the Wire Kickstarter Funds, Opens Late Pledges
item.dc:creator: Matthias Ashmoor
item.description: Kazmo Studios' tactical sandbox RPG Outside the Wire beat its Kickstarter goal in under three hours. Late pledges for the Deluxe Box Set are open now.
item.content:encoded:
AT THE ASHFORGE — Outside the Wire, the tactical sandbox tabletop RPG from Kazmo Studios, closed its Kickstarter campaign on October 1 well past its goal, and late pledges are now open. A disclosure before the specs: I'm the lead editor on this book. The numbers below come from the campaign page, the studio, and outside outlets, so you can check every one of them.

The game was designed by Derek Roberson, a retired US Marine whose 35 years of service included Desert Storm and Fallujah, Geek Native reports. Players run a small unit through asymmetric counterinsurgency operations, and the sandbox tracks three numbers as they go: Local Trust, Command Confidence, and Insurgent Activity. Checks are a 2d10 roll-under. There are no hit points; wounds come from an Individual Effects Table. It plays with a GM or solo, the solo side driven by reactive encounter cards and automata flowsheets. Roberson told Wazza's Whimsical Wanderings that non-violent actions can do more good than violence, and added a warning: "The combat is deadly; enter at your own peril."

The order slip

  • Goal: $10,000, reached in under three hours (Geek Native)
  • Pledged: $74,464 from 824 backers, per the Kickstarter page as of October 14, with eight stretch goals unlocked during the campaign (Kazmo Studios)
  • Core rulebook: hardback, more than 300 pages, with real-world regional profiles and three operational sandbox settings
  • Campaign tiers: $18 for the digital Ambush at Dawn starter set, $25 for the core rulebook PDF, $50 for the hardback, up to $110 for the Deluxe Box Set
  • Delivery: digital rewards from November 2026; physical books and boxed sets in April and May 2027

Late pledges run through the same Kickstarter page. Kazmo's announcement features the Deluxe Box Set (the physical core rulebook, campaign trackers, punchboard combatant tokens, and regional grid maps) with every digital stretch goal from the campaign included: the scenarios Drop Dead Echo, Red Lantern Boondoggle, and Scorpion's Nest, plus tactical map packs and one-page missions. An official Foundry VTT module is an optional add-on. The studio hasn't posted a closing date.

The design borrows from older military games, Twilight: 2000, MERC, and Recon among them, and the far tables that grew up on those will know the shape of it. Anyone who wants to try before pledging can start with The Shepherd's Transit, a free quickstart scenario listed on the official Outside the Wire site.

— M.A., from the forge

item.title: Gelatinous Cube Found in Tavern Walk-In, Inspector Says
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A gelatinous cube was found in the walk-in cooler of Brindlemoor's Sleeping Mule tavern. The inspector marked the cheese 'unverified.'
item.content:encoded:
THE SLEEPING MULE TAVERN, BRINDLEMOOR, CELLAR LEVEL — A gelatinous cube was found living in the walk-in cooler of this Tanner's Row tavern during a routine inspection Tuesday. It had been there, by the keeper's best estimate, since the spring turnip delivery.

Inspector Corwin Tallowby of the Brindlemoor Public Cellars Board opened the cooler door at 10:40 a.m. and recorded a cube ten feet on a side, transparent, and holding most of the week's order. Visible inside: two wheels of cheese, a ham, a ladle, a pair of spectacles, and a sleeping apprentice cook named Dunmar, whom the cube had not finished with.

Dunmar is at full hit points, 19 of 19, and slightly pickled. "It was warm in there," he told this reporter. "Warmer than the kitchen."

Keeper Bess Harrowgate said the cube had been "a good tenant." It kept the cooler spotless and never once asked for a raise. "I thought the shelves were just very clean," she said. Tallowby noted that the shelves were also gone.

Under the Cellars Board code, a tavern may hold one gelatinous cube on the premises provided it is kept below the cheese line and listed on the menu. The Sleeping Mule had done neither. Tallowby issued a Class Two citation, marked the cheese "unverified," and gave the keeper ten days to remove the cube or reclassify it as a dessert.

Removal is the sticking point. The Fourth Attempt, who were drinking in the taproom, were approached for a quote and a quick delve. The party's bard, who asked to be named, declined. "We do dungeons," he said. "This is a cooler." The fighter added that the last time they were hired for kitchen work, they lost a mule. The mule turned up later, unharmed and well fed, which she says is worse.

I held out the ten-foot pole from the cellar steps, as is my habit, and rolled poorly. The cube took the pole whole. That is my eighth of the season, and the first I have lost to something that was already refrigerated.

Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society has been informed. An adjuster said spoiled inventory is covered but "inventory that has become a roommate" is under review. Reeve Fennick's office would only say, "We are aware of the cube." Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called it "a Level Two matter that was visiting," despite the cooler being above ground.

The Sleeping Mule remains open. Cold cuts are off the menu. The cube is, for now, the cold cuts.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: 4,917 Lottery Tickets Win on Triple Zeros in Carolan Reach
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: Lottery officials in the Carolan Reach say 4,917 tickets hit triple zeros, a 1.7 million gp bill. Skritch smells a rigged die. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the third bell after midnight, the Carolan Reach Schoolhouse Raffle Office announced that the night's lottery drawing had come up triple zeros, and that 4,917 tickets had allegedly won. That is a lot of winners for one set of bones. The Lower City, where I keep my sources, has talked of nothing else since.

The Raffle Office runs a daily game called Pick-Three Bones, in which three numbered knucklebones are rolled and anyone who guessed them in order collects. On Monday night all three bones landed on zero. Each winning ticket pays 500 gp or 250 gp, depending on whether the player wagered a silver or two. The total bill comes to roughly 1.7 million gp. The Office says it will pay every coin. Allegedly cheerfully.

'Triples are combinations of three of the same numbers,' an Office spokesperson explained, in case anyone was confused about what a triple is. 'They are some of the most popular sets of numbers among players.' This is apparently the reason so many ticket holders chose them. It is also the reason the Office now owns a very large debt.

I tracked down Marlo Pettibone, a Lower City cobbler, who was holding a sausage on a stick when I found him. 'I play triple zeros every night,' he said. 'Eleven years. My wife says it is a sickness. My wife is now getting a new roof.' He then asked me not to print where the roof will go, and I will not, except that it is allegedly the one over the Copper Kettle.

Not everyone cheered. A sour man in a good hat from the Tower District sniffed that the whole thing 'smells like a rigged die.' The Office denies this. The bones, it says, were inspected by three clerks and one goat, all of whom signed.

Anyway. There was a really lovely silver button in the gutter outside the Raffle Office, and I spent a good ten minutes with it. Where was I. Right. The odds.

Nobody printed the odds, so I asked a tavern bookmaker, who said, 'Low.' I asked another, who said 'also low, but people love zeros.' Between them they seem to have worked out why a realm of gamblers keeps backing the same boring numbers: it feels like a secret and everybody has the same one. A pigeon watching from a ledge appeared to disagree. I did not engage with the pigeon.

The Office says the winners can collect at any raffle counter in the Reach, and the schoolhouses that the lottery funds are expected to stay open. Allegedly. Meanwhile, 4,917 households are lighter by one lottery ticket and heavier by a few hundred gp, and one cobbler's wife is reading roofing catalogues.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Alfalfa Sprout Recall: 76 Sick, Brother Wendell Boils Soup
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: An alfalfa sprout recall has sickened 76 across 16 provinces. Brother Wendell would like everyone to step away from the jar and put on a pot of soup.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, an alfalfa sprout recall is spreading through the realm, and 76 people across 16 provinces have now taken ill after eating the little green fuzz. The Potion & Provisions Authority and the Disease Council say the trouble traces back to nine hundred and fifty pounds of sprouting seed sold by Barleyn Seeds of Millersburrow, in Ohyo Vale.

The old herbals have always been a bit wary of anything grown warm, wet, and in the dark for a week. Sprouts are exactly that: a spa for seeds, and apparently for a bloody-flux sprite and a belly pox called Agona. The new studies agree with the herbals, which is rare enough that I wrote it on the temple wall.

Here is what the Authority found. A supplier traced the seed to a grower whose sprouts were already under investigation. A sample of spent soak-water from one lot tested positive for the sprite. The seed went out between the second week of Frostfall's cousin, February, and late August, in quarter-pound pouches up to fifty-pound sacks, to forty-two provinces. The big sacks carry lot code SAL2-24JB, bottom right corner of the label. The small pouches carry nothing at all, which I find unkind.

Symptoms run from cramps and sickness to the bloody sort, and in the worst cases the kidneys give out. Little ones, elders, and anyone whose humors are already poorly should take extra care. If you ate the sprouts and feel wretched, see a healer. Do not wait it out with a heroic attitude.

The Authority's advice is plain. Do not sprout it, plant it, sell it, or give it to a neighbor. Seal it in a bag and throw it out. Scrub every jar, tray, and countertop it touched. Barleyn Seeds says its other products are fine and is offering refunds, though I would not blame anyone for glaring at the whole shelf for a while.

A woman called Odalie Pennywort, a market-stall greengrocer in the Lower City, told me she had a window-sill of sprouts going for a month. 'They looked so healthy,' she said. 'Then I read the notice and gave the jar a funeral.' A good funeral, I told her. She had the right of it.

I have been at this a while, and the lesson never changes: the things that look the healthiest on the plate are often the ones nobody has cooked. Heat is the oldest remedy we have. It is also why I keep going on about the pot. (Last month it was the dairy cows. Before that, the storm. Something is always sprouting.) My friend Nyx tells me there is a gadget that grows sprouts on a schedule with a glowing app. Go outside, Nyx.

Today's soup is a simple cabbage-and-white-bean with plenty of garlic, boiled hard. Cooked greens are safe greens. No sprouts required, and your kidneys will thank you.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Trade Deal Reached After Two-Day Parley; Hybrid Carriages Cut
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: A preliminary trade deal between the Sembian Concord and Kara-Tur trims carriage imports and secures rare-earth ore. Twenty-seven realms must still sign.
item.content:encoded:
The Sembian Concord and Kara-Tur struck a preliminary trade deal on Tuesday after two days of talks over trade imbalances. The terms: lower tariffs on some Concord goods entering Kara-Tur, steadier shipments of rare-earth ore, and a cut of up to half in Kara-Tur's hybrid carriages rolling into Concord markets.

The parley ran two days. I have covered sieges that ended faster and with less paperwork. The opening handshake between Trade Envoy Marosh Sefkovitch and Minister Wan Wentoe lasted two seconds. Firm. No hidden dagger detected. The ore, however, was clearly on the table, and it was not subtle about it.

Here is the situation on the ground. For years the Concord has watched Kara-Tur's carriages, the kind that run on both enchanted charge and ordinary oats, roll in cheap and in great numbers. The Concord answered with tariffs. Kara-Tur answered with its grip on rare-earth ore, the dull grey rocks that every enchanted engine in the Realms quietly depends on. Each side was holding the other's supply line. That is a siege, whatever the diplomats call it.

Wan Wentoe told reporters his empire was a partner in solving the Concord's problems, not the root of them. I have heard this line from besieging armies before. It usually arrives right before the ladders do.

The deal is not final. Every one of the Concord's twenty-seven member realms must approve it, and the Concord has never once agreed on lunch. Sefkovitch will brief the realm leaders in Ordulin next week. Expect a long parley. Expect speeches. Expect one small realm to demand an exemption for its cheese.

Meanwhile the ordinary carriage-buyer, the merchant who just wants a cheap ride to market, will learn what this cost him only when the price tags change. Nobody in the pavilion was asked what he wanted. Nobody ever is.

I give the tension eleven siege-days, down from twenty-two. The truce is real. The ore still has not shipped. Peace in trade is the same as peace in war: it lasts until the first shipment is late.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: SpellX Seeks 40 Billion gp Loan for Envydia Rune-Chips
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: SpellX wants a 40 billion gp loan to buy Envydia's AI chips, and Nyx is thrilled, solvent in spirit, and already smelling smoke.
item.content:encoded:
OKAY. SpellX, the astral-rocket guild, is borrowing 40 billion gp to buy more AI chips from Envydia, the Salmon Scroll reports, and I have never been so jealous of a debt in my life. About 10 billion gp comes from bank vaults and 30 billion from investment-grade bonds, with the closing date set for 2027.

Apollyon Grand Holdings, the lender with the worst name in the realm, is leading the financing. Pimcrow Bond Guild is said to be among the small circle of lenders at the table. Nobody has signed anything yet, which in my experience is when a deal looks its prettiest.

Let me explain why I'm excited. Envydia's rune-chips are the finest mana throughput money can buy, and SpellX has been stacking them like firewood. Guildmaster Elon Muskrat's treasurer says the guild passed 1.4 gigawatts of arcane compute last quarter and expects to top 2 by year's end. He also says new compute "has paid back in less than a year." I wrote that on my wrist so I could show Byte. Byte, my pseudodragon, replied, "Ask about our low-interest scrying plans!" Which is not what I asked.

The sums are enormous. SpellX spent about 18 billion gp on capital projects in one quarter, nearly 16 billion of it on chips. It already holds roughly 100 billion gp in cash and bonds after its big public listing, so naturally it is asking for 40 billion more. I would call that sound planning, except that the rest of the realm's lenders are getting nervous about funding the great chip race, and a sage of the counting-houses figures the AI buildout needs 1.5 trillion gp of outside money by 2028. Somebody has to hold the coin purse, and apparently it's whoever answers the door at Apollyon.

On the trading floor, SpellX shares slipped two percent after the news and Envydia ticked up half a percent. That's the market for you: the chip forge gets a standing order, the borrower gets a flinch. I also noticed the guild expects over 100 billion gp in annual revenue by December, a number that sounds great until you remember I once expected my self-driving carriage to stop at the school.

Would I join the bond? Yes. Would I read the terms? I have read terms before. My left eyebrow is still in one of them.

Verdict: four out of five beholder eyes. The fifth is reserved for when the chips arrive and the first runic latency test doesn't set the vault on fire.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below. Burns sustained: 1. Bonds purchased: 0, for lack of coin. Eyebrows: pending.

item.title: 300,000 Public Workers Down Tools Across the Moonshae Isles
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: A public-sector strike of 300,000 clerics, teachers and clerks hit the Moonshae Isles over pay, and the Treasury's reply was an offer to talk.
item.content:encoded:
Three hundred thousand public workers walked out today in a public-sector strike. That's the story.

Clerics, teachers, court scribes and infirmary hands across the Moonshae Isles downed tools for twenty-four hours over pay. The guild treaty ran out in Midsummer, prices kept climbing, and the unions say wages are now five to seven percent behind. Essential services keep running. Everything else sits there, wondering where everyone went.

Royal Minister Jack Chamberlock, keeper of the realm's purse, answered with a letter. He offered talks at the Hall of Workplace Parley, warning of "great disruption to the public, especially the most vulnerable." The Treasury also points out that it has set aside 1.2 billion gp for public pay, which it calls "significant." Significant is a word you use when you want to avoid saying a number someone can check.

The unions turned the offer down fast. Shop Steward Kevan Callinhorn, chair of the Moonshae Congress of Trade Guilds, said the offer "cannot see how it represents any change" in the Minister's position.

Here is the sticking point. The unions want pay on the table. The Minister says pay can be discussed "alongside other matters." That means he'll talk about anything except the thing you came to talk about. It's like inviting a hungry dwarf to supper and offering to discuss tablecloths.

"I teach forty children arithmetic, and the arithmetic of my own wages is the hardest lesson I give," said Orla Brindlehammer, a village schoolmistress, standing at a picket line outside the Hall of Letters. "Nobody in the Treasury has ever failed that class. They've never had to sit it."

Palace sources say a neutral mediator may be called in, but not until at least one strike day has passed. So they want the strike to hurt first. Fine. Further single-day stoppages are already scheduled over the next eight days, and the unions say nobody is bluffing.

The Minister's department and the unions are no longer on speaking terms, which makes the offer of talks the one thing both sides agree is odd. I've covered the Golden Coast clerks calling their first strike. Different realm, same Treasury energy.

Public workers keep the roads mapped, the sick tended and the children able to count. They are asking for pay that keeps up with bread. That isn't a radical position. It's a ledger.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: 4.5 Million Grill Brush Recall Is Just a Bristle Pivot
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Wallmart Bazaar recalls 4.5 million grill brushes that shed wire bristles into dinner. Sterling Vanmoor sees a bold new fiber strategy.
item.content:encoded:
Wallmart Bazaar is recalling nearly 4.5 million grill brushes after the Royal Commission on Consumer Peril warned that their wire bristles can come loose, stick to the grate, and end up in your dinner. Some people call that a product recall. I call it the most ambitious fiber-enrichment initiative in the history of the Guilds.

The brushes, sold under the Adept Grill label from January 2021 through August 2026, ran between 1 and 28 gp, alone or in tool sets. The Peril Commission says a swallowed bristle can mean serious internal injury and surgery. No injuries have been reported so far. Disruptors never get that kind of runway.

Let us unpack the numbers. Four and a half million units. Five and a half years of sales. That is a distribution network most founders would sell a kidney for, and I say that as a man who has, in a manner of speaking, sold a kidney. (It was a mimic kidney. Long story.) Wallmart now offers a full refund or store credit. That is not a recall. That is a customer re-engagement funnel with a built-in repeat purchase.

Some will call this a failure of quality control. Those people have never rightsized an entire shipping fleet before breakfast. Bristle shedding is simply product-to-plate integration, and frankly, other cookware guilds are years behind. I am told Wallmart's Guildmaster, whom I met once at a gala in the Yawning Portal, has not commented. That is leadership. You do not comment. You pivot.

Regulators will, of course, call this a safety hazard. Regulators always do. I would note that the Peril Commission only learned of this because someone had to read a report, and nobody has ever grown a guild by reading reports. Meanwhile the humble grill brush, much like the humble adventurer, was never meant to be loved. It was meant to scale.

Customers should stop using the brushes at once and contact Wallmart for the refund. I recommend doing it before your 5 a.m. sword routine, when your head is clear and your gizzard is empty.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • A recall is just a sale with a second act.
  • If your product sheds, your product is generous.
  • Never read the safety report. Be the safety report.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Inflation Hits 3.7% as Lamp Oil Jumps 9%, Loaf Index Wobbles
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: The September inflation report shows prices up 3.7% in a year, with lamp oil doing half the damage. Barnaby Tallowmere checks his flour sacks again.
item.content:encoded:
The Royal Bureau of Labor Tallies released its September inflation report Wednesday, and prices rose 3.7% over the past twelve months, up from 3.4% in August. Prices rose 0.6% in September alone. (I have checked this four times. I checked it a fifth time against a sack of flour, which was not helpful, but it was comforting.)

The villain is lamp oil. It jumped 9.1% in the month and accounted for about half the entire increase, because the Hormoth Narrows remain shut while Calimshan and the realm keep up their seven-month war. Oil is the one price that sneaks into every other price. It lights the tavern, powers the wagon that carries the grain, and heats the oven that makes the loaf. Energy overall rose 5.2%.

Here is the part that made me sit down. Strip out food and energy and the core rate was 2.6% a year, a little hotter than the 2.5% the clerks of the counting houses had guessed. That matters because the Federal Reserve of Waterdeep watches the core figure. As I explained when borrowing costs hit a 24-year high, Reserve Governor Kristoff Wallop has already said more hikes are needed. Traders now give a December hike something like 88% odds. The Reserve meets October 27 and 28, where it is expected to hold.

On the Loaf Index, one honest loaf is still 6 copper. I want to be clear about that. But a 3.7% rise means that a year ago the same loaf cost about 5.8 copper, and a hireling's wages have to outrun that gap before they get to feel any better. The hirelings of the realm added just 29,000 jobs last month, so I am not optimistic about the race. And the hearth-loan rates are already at 7.40%, so nobody can borrow their way out of it either.

Governor Wallop says the climbing yields reflect a stronger economy, not fear of rising prices, and that inflation expectations are "well anchored." Perhaps so. An anchor is a fine thing for a ship. My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, notes that a boot has no anchor and also no interest, and she has asked me to stop calling her at night.

Here is the economics underneath, plainly. When the price of one thing rises sharply, it pulls the average up even if nothing else changed. Whether it spreads depends on whether merchants and workers start expecting more and raising their own prices. That is what the Reserve is trying to prevent, and the only tool it has is making borrowing expensive. It works slowly and it hurts the tavern-keepers first.

What this means for your pantry: buy the flour now, buy the lamp oil later if you can wait, and do not ask anyone who says the market will sort itself out.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Johnstone: Midterm Polls Wrong, and He Stays Speaker Anyway
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: Speaker Johnstone says the midterm polls are wrong and he will lead the Red Oliphants even if they lose the Commons. The lawn business is on hold.
item.content:encoded:
Speaker Mikel Johnstone told the realm this week that the midterm elections will go the Red Oliphants' way, that the polls saying otherwise are wrong, and that if they lose the Chamber of Commons he intends to stay on as their leader regardless. He delivered the first claim to the Foxfire Tidings and the second to the Cauldron Broadcasting Society. Both were described as confident.

Readers of the minutes will recall that Johnstone previously mused about returning to Shrievesport to start a lawn business should the majority slip. He has since called the remark "tongue in cheek." I have checked the transcript. The tongue is not visible, but the cheek is.

The procedure here deserves explanation, because the gentleman from the Bayou is counting on it. A party that loses the Commons does not automatically lose its leader. It loses the gavel, the committee chairs, the good office with the window, and the power to schedule anything. The leader keeps his title, which is now a title for a man who sits in the minority and objects. Johnstone calls this "stay and serve." The Chamber's rulebook calls it Tuesday.

His case against the polls is historical. A rival crier house, he noted, has conceded that the Oliphants were undercounted in the autumn polls in fourteen of the last sixteen elections. That is accurate as far as it goes. It does not mention the two elections in which they were counted correctly and the Oliphants lost, which is where the lawn business came from.

Meanwhile the Speaker is touring forty districts across twenty-two provinces, having raised "millions" for the cause. He reminds listeners that he defended High Lord Donwald of the Golden Towers through two impeachment trials, which he offers as a qualification. The war in Calimshan, the price of lamp oil, and the High Lord's own standing in the provinces he is visiting go unmentioned.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the Oliphants' internal count is "better than the public one, and the public one is a cliff." Asked what the internal count says, the courtier said it was "a rumor with a spreadsheet."

For the record, the Promises Made / Promises Kept tally stands at: Made, "I will be Speaker for at least two more years," "the polling is wrong," and "heaven forbid." Kept: the one about touring, which is going ahead. The tally is not close.

The Commons will be decided on the third of next month. Until then the Speaker remains optimistic, the polls remain wrong, and the lawn business remains, in his words, a joke. The motion carried. Nobody read it.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Rust Monster Eats Shears at Undermaw Level Seven Opening
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A rust monster ate the ribbon shears, a stair gate, and the Reeve's chain at the Undermaw Level Seven opening. Chapter 9 says it's on track.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 6 — A rust monster ate the ceremonial ribbon shears, then the stair gate, then most of Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor's chain of office yesterday morning. That ended the third annual grand opening of Level Seven about four minutes after it began.

Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9 has promised for three autumns running that the Undermaw's seventh level will open to licensed parties "next tenday." About two hundred townsfolk turned up to watch, along with a brass band and a refreshment table run by four hirelings, who were paid in coupons.

The rust monster came up the stairwell during the second verse of the Guild anthem. Witnesses say it went for the shears first. The Reeve was holding them. "I felt them go warm, and then I felt them go," said Reeve Fennick. The gate's hinges followed, then the gate, then the clasp of her chain. "We are aware of the rust monster," she told this reporter, holding the remaining links.

The Fourth Attempt, invited to descend first, took the worst of it. Box score: fighter 44 of 44 hit points, armor class down from 18 to 11 after her plate became what she called "a fine orange powder"; wizard 22 of 22, one dagger short; mule 11 of 11, carrying nothing made of iron and not at all sorry. The party's bard, who asked to be named, called it "a very expensive way to find out what's down there."

The band's tuba section came through untouched. Bandleader Orrin Tuck credited brass being "the wrong sort of metal." The drummer's rim hoops were not so lucky.

I lost my seventh ten-foot pole of the season at the foot of the stairs. I rolled poorly: I held it out to see if the creature was a mimic. It took the iron tip and left me the wood, which I am told is the polite thing.

Chapter 9 says nothing has changed. "Level Seven remains on track to open next tenday," said Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick. "The rust monster is a Level Six matter that was visiting." A Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society adjuster, speaking on condition that nobody ask her about the ribbon, said the fighter's armor will be filed as wear and tear. The shears are listed as a "ribbon-related incident, pending."

Wooden replacement shears have been ordered. As of press time the rust monster was asleep across the top step, which Chapter 9 describes as "a soft launch."

— H.D., filing from below
